Quick interim report before I write the LaTeX — three things from the checks turned out to matter for the text:

1. **Item 0.3 needs a slightly stronger fix than the checklist says.** The certified "Weyl–Schur margin" *m* is what the head block clears after subtracting κ²/d_tail, but the exact block-Schur condition for Q ⪰ c·I is (λ_head − c)(d_tail − c) ≥ κ², i.e. c + κ²/(d_tail − c) ≤ λ_head. Solving gives c = m − κ²m/(d(d−m)) ≈ m − 4.0×10⁻⁸. So the coercivity constant §8.6 may use is **6.1159×10⁻⁴** (even) and 5.2613×10⁻² (odd), not 6.11635×10⁻⁴. Harmless for the theorem, but I'll state it as a lemma with the corrected constant rather than assert Q ⪰ m·I.

2. **Item 0.4 (pin "equivalent").** Suzuki [1] Prop. 1.2 reads: for ω₀ > 0, ζ(s) ≠ 0 for Re s > 1/2+ω₀ ⟺ Θ_ω is meromorphic inner for **every** ω > ω₀. The single-shift "equivalence" in §1.1 isn't his statement; I'll rewrite §1.1 and the abstract around the exact one.

3. **§9.3 is out of date.** Suzuki's Lemma 4.4 (hypothesis "ω > 1/2 and a > 1") already proves ‖H_{ω,a}‖ < 1 for every finite section in the classical range, via his Lemma 4.3 support argument plus compactness. That is the Paley–Wiener step §9.3 says was "not reproduced" — it's in [1]. I'll cite it and reposition Theorem A as the complementary 0 < ω ≤ 1/2 result.

The scaffold is delivered above. Here is the structure and the reasoning behind it.

## Recommended layout

```
shifted-zeta-program/
├── README.md · CITATION.cff · CHANGELOG.md · CONTRIBUTING.md · MANIFEST.md
├── LICENSE-CC-BY-4.0.md (text)  ·  LICENSE-MIT (code)
├── .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/{verification-report,possible-error}.md · workflows/build-latex.yml
├── papers/            one folder per manuscript; source+PDF only when released
│   ├── first-slab-positivity/   ← the deposit bundle, complete
│   ├── shifted-screw-margin/    STATUS.md   (Paper 1, 21 pp., author block empty)
│   ├── shifted-zeta-string/     STATUS.md   (Paper 2, v5 frozen 28 Aug pending human review)
│   ├── defect-depth/            STATUS.md   (Paper 3, draft v1, every bib entry %% VERIFY)
│   └── offaxis-detector/        STATUS.md   (earlier thread; interval port outstanding)
├── verification/      the audit trail: CHECKLIST (renumbered to v1.0), referee-round records, recomputation scripts
├── notes/             the research log, flat, original filenames; README indexes ~45 notes by thread with one-liners
├── code/              labs/ihara, labs/tower; certificates/first-slab is release-gated behind D1–D5
├── references/        bibliography of what was used; third-party PDFs are never committed
└── environment/       pinned mpmath/numpy/scipy
```

Three design choices worth flagging. First, `papers/` separates *released* from *status-only* folders, because the companion drafts have passed internal rounds but not external review and all four still have empty author blocks; the STATUS files carry exactly what each needs before release, drawn from ROUND19, PROGRESS, ROUND6_closeout and the .tex headers. Second, `notes/` stays flat with original filenames so the dense cross-references inside the round reports keep resolving; the README does the grouping (physics routes → pivot at ROUND12 → screw margin → string → Ihara lab → first slab) and states plainly that it includes closed routes and one same-day retraction. Third, `verification/` is a first-class directory rather than an appendix, since verification-by-others is the project's actual plan — the checklist, both review records, the issue templates and CONTRIBUTING's five house rules (run the control, search before claiming novelty, read the printed PDF, verify object type, keep the ledger accurate — all lifted from failures recorded in the notes) are built around that.

**One thing to decide before tagging anything.** The Zenodo–GitHub integration archives the *whole repository* at a release, which conflicts with your preprint-only deposit if the notes and companion status files are already committed. The README spells out the two clean options: a small dedicated repository for the paper (exactly the contents of `papers/first-slab-positivity/`, which is already self-contained with its own license and metadata) linked from this program repo, or tagging v1.0 here before anything else is added. I'd take the first.

**What I did not include.** The forty-odd existing notes, the four unreleased .tex files and the lab code are not in the zip — re-emitting them risks transcription slips in documents that are records. `MANIFEST.md` maps each project document to its destination path, names the one file to rename (the round-1 review), and lists the reproduction scripts that were never saved to the project and would need recovering. The third-party PDFs are listed in `references/README.md` and excluded by `.gitignore`.

The README, manifest and renumbered checklist are also saved in the RH3 project.

parts:
I think it's the right call, and your two reasons are the strong ones: a single repo is what the formalization crowd actually works with (one clone, one issue tracker, one dependency graph across papers), and the per-paper repo overhead would be real for five manuscripts that cite each other and share a research log. Three things worth getting right so the single repo doesn't cost you what the split would have bought.

**Citation and discoverability.** "Title + folder + Zenodo DOI" works, with one refinement: cite the *version* DOI, not the concept DOI, so a citation pins the content (`papers/first-slab-positivity/` at v1.0 is a fixed object; the concept DOI always resolves to the newest release). The one thing you lose is that indexers (Google Scholar, OpenAlex) see a Zenodo record titled "Shifted zeta program", not the paper's title and abstract. The cheap fix is to *also* upload each released paper's PDF as its own Zenodo record when it's ready — a ten-minute manual upload with the paper's `.zenodo.json`, no code — and link the two records with Zenodo's related-identifiers field (the paper record `isPartOf` the repo record; the repo `hasPart` the paper). You get one repository, per-paper DOIs with correct metadata, and every path resolves to the same content.

**What goes into the v1.0 snapshot.** The Zenodo integration archives everything at the tag, so the earlier "preprint only" constraint becomes a decision about what's committed at tag time rather than about repository boundaries. My suggestion: the preprint bundle, `verification/`, the status files for the four companions (not their `.tex` — empty author blocks and `%% VERIFY` bibliographies shouldn't be in a DOI'd object), and the notes *after a redaction pass*. That pass matters. The notes were written as session reports and contain material that is fine in a private project and not fine in a public archive: the draft letter to Suzuki (PROGRESS §4b), the outreach shortlist with personal characterizations of named people (ROUND19 §5), and a "fatally flawed, do not cite" verdict on a specific named paper (BRIEF_three_live_routes §3.5). Scrub those, add a one-paragraph preface saying the notes are LLM-written round reports produced under your direction, and they become the kind of candid research log that formalization and informal-math communities genuinely value — retractions included.

**Making it legible to formalizers.** What that community wants is a precise statement inventory with a dependency graph and per-statement status, which is exactly what Appendix C of the preprint gestures at. I'd add a `blueprint/` directory (leanblueprint-compatible later) with each theorem and lemma stated self-contained and its status marked *proved on paper / numerically certified / formalized*, plus a machine-readable `statements/ledger.yaml`. And be candid about feasibility: Lemma 7.1 (block-Schur) is finite-dimensional linear algebra and would formalize in Mathlib in an afternoon; Lemma 6.1's polynomial sign analysis is `nlinarith`/`positivity` territory; the Volterra identities are moderate; Prop. 4.2 needs the digamma integral representation, which I'd want to check Mathlib's coverage of before promising; Theorem B is a certificate-plus-checker problem in the Flyspeck style (large but well-defined once the Arb results are released as data); Theorem C's strong-operator machinery is out of reach for now. Saying that up front is what makes people pick up the easy items.

If you want, I'll update the scaffold accordingly: rewrite the deposit-policy section for the single-repo plan, add a root `.zenodo.json` with the related-identifier links and per-paper citation blocks, add the `blueprint/` and `statements/` skeletons with the ledger populated from the preprint, and write the notes redaction checklist as a file.

The review was sound, and its changes are now in your repo folder (24 files, nothing git-committed by me). Here's the outcome.

**What I confirmed independently before applying anything.** The patch applies cleanly to your first commit `50cb4d2`, which is exactly what your checkout is at. The CFF finding is real: the CFF 1.2.0 schema only allows `software` or `dataset` at top level, and your paper's `CITATION.cff` failed with `type: generic`; the proposed replacements both validate against the official schema. The new numerical script is faithful to the paper — its impulse formula matches eq. (kappa-explicit) and its Galerkin overlap/index algebra is right — and it runs 16/16 under the pinned Python 3.12 environment; an injected 0.001 error produces four FAILs and exit 1, so CI can fail. The license, "no error survives" rewording, and the notes-index correction were all accurate.

**Where I deviated from the patch.** The reviewer hard-coded `50cb4d22…` into the README citation blocks; a file can't cite the commit that contains it, so I used a commit-based interim form with a ⟨hash⟩ placeholder plus DOI templates with ⟨…⟩ fields, and removed every `NNNNNNN`-style placeholder. The review-dated "state at the 9 September review" paragraphs in README/RELEASING were folded into durable statements. The reviewer's `.zenodo.json` description contained an instruction to you ("confirm before depositing") that would have been deposited verbatim — that moved to RELEASING's gate step, and the deposit description was rewritten to be true at tag time. The rest was taken as-is, plus a few consistency fixes on top (stale "dual license" wording, the `code/certificates/` README still carrying your work address, `papers/README.md` now says no tag or DOI exists yet).

**The certificate candidate is the big news.** It stays out of the tree (D1–D5 still open, as the reviewer and your own gate say), but I went further than the review did: I regenerated all three Investigations from scratch in a fresh pinned environment (python-flint 0.9.0 etc., about four minutes total) and every result table came out byte-identical to the archived ones — kernel-norm enclosure `0.012293050401142319 ± 6.8e-19`, 512 boxes, margins `6.116350109501e-4 / 5.261670009275e-2`, exactly the preprint's constants. That's recorded as `verification/first-slab/CERTIFICATE_RERUN_20260909.md` and noted at D4 in the checklist and VERIFICATION_STATUS. The gap to code release is now D1, D2, D3 and the stale write-up passages (D5).

Two things for you: move the new workflow (`mv _github/workflows/check-first-slab.yml .github/workflows/ && rm -r _github`), and the reviewer's suggestion to publish the handoff itself under `notes/repository-review/` is a judgement call I left to you. A full response table is saved in the project as `REVIEW_RESPONSE_repository_review_20260909.md`.

archive_metadata.format: ChatGPT-style conversation mapping; local conversion, not an official provider export
archive_metadata.source_kind: Claude Cowork cloud session event log (claude.ai GET /v1/code/sessions/{id}/events), read in the signed-in browser and reduced to completed public messages
archive_metadata.message_timestamps: Event times, in seconds since Unix epoch and ISO 8601: the session's own timestamp where the event carries one, otherwise the server's event time (typed messages); the conversation create_time is the session's creation time in the session list
archive_metadata.coverage: Messages typed by the person (including any sent while a reply was in progress, with the names of files sent with them) and interruption markers; the options the person selected in question cards; the assistant text shown in the chat: progress lines between tool calls, question cards rendered as text, notes and file-card captions sent through tools (phase commentary), and the text ending each completed turn (phase final_answer); recorded through the event log as read
omitted_record_types: system, developer and harness text (reminders, date notes, memory snapshots, continuation summaries, hook feedback, skill text, local command output)
tool calls and outputs, except the chat-visible items named in coverage
permission prompts, control and environment events, usage and cost figures
attachment contents (file names are kept in message metadata)

session.title_source: the session's title in the Cowork session list

source_events.read_by: Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) in Claude Cowork, via Claude in Chrome
source_events.note: sha256_of_events_json is the SHA-256 of JSON.stringify(events sorted by sequence_num) computed in the browser; neither the event log nor the events file is stored in the repository, since they hold instructions, reasoning and tool traffic that the coverage rules exclude
